objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe every IFR weather source and product this Task lists at instructor depth, say plainly which listed charts the current Aviation Weather Handbook no longer describes and what to teach instead, decode the handbook's own sample reports aloud, and build a learner's IFR go/no-go weather briefing skill from rote decoding to a correlated decision.
why: Before an IFR flight the pilot in command must become familiar with weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements and the alternatives if the flight cannot be completed [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]]. The products keep changing: the AIM warns that new products and the termination of some legacy products can cause confusion, and that every weather decision must rest on all available pertinent products [[34:62|AIM 7-1-3]]. An overly simple understanding of weather often leads inexperienced learners into situations they did not expect [[25:84|AIH 3-33]], so your job is to teach the learner to connect the products into one decision, not just to decode them.

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner hands you tomorrow's briefing and says, "Destination TAF is 1,500 overcast, so we're good." She has not looked at the freezing level, the PIREPs or the AIRMETs, and the airplane is not approved for icing. What would you ask her first, and how would you get her to find the problem herself instead of telling her?

key_terms.def: Automated surface observing systems. ASOS is the nation's primary surface observing network; AWOS is similar but generally reports fewer elements and may have less sensor backup [[28:286|AWH 24-2]] [[28:287|AWH 24-3]].
The age of weather data, from the event to its display in the cockpit or on the EFB; it may limit how a product can be used [[28:25|AWH 3-2]].
A briefing that meets the preflight rule. Pilots may get one from online resources without contacting Flight Service [[28:26|AWH 3-3]].
The routine surface report made near the top of each hour, and the unscheduled special report made when set criteria are met between hours [[28:290|AWH 24-6]].
The lowest layer aloft reported as broken or overcast, or the vertical visibility into a total obscuration [[28:300|AWH 24-16]].
A forecast for the area within 5 SM of the center of the runway complex, usually for 24 hours and for some major airports 30 [[28:407|AWH 27-6]].

The AWC web tool showing observations, forecasts and warnings from 14 hours past to 15 hours ahead [[34:63|AIM 7-1-4]]; with its static images it replaced the text area forecast for the CONUS [[28:425|AWH 27-24]].
A pilot weather report, routine (UA) or urgent (UUA). Altitudes are MSL unless noted [[28:310|AWH 24-26]] [[28:311|AWH 24-27]].
The SIGMET, Convective SIGMET, AIRMET and CWA: forecasts that advise en route aircraft of potentially hazardous weather [[34:68|AIM 7-1-6]] [[34:69|AIM 7-1-6]].
The lowest altitude over a location at which the air temperature reaches 0 °C [[28:365|AWH 25-23]].
A prog chart of flight categories, turbulence and freezing levels up to FL240 at 12 and 24 hours; in-flight icing is not shown [[28:436|AWH 27-35]] [[28:437|AWH 27-36]].
The SPC product showing the potential for severe and general thunderstorms over the next eight days, with risk categories from MRGL to HIGH [[28:457|AWH 27-56]].

chunks.title: What this Task asks of an instrument instructor

body.p: The PTS objective is instructional knowledge of IFR weather information: the sources of weather and the reports and charts listed in the Task (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area III, Task A). If current weather is not available or does not suit the scenario, the evaluator simulates the reports and forecasts (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area III, Task A, NOTE). The Instrument lesson IR.I.B covers the pilot's side of this subject, including alternates and weather theory; this lesson adds how to teach it and how the products have changed.

The AWH sorts weather information into five types: observations, analyses, advisories, forecasts and tools [[28:285|AWH 24-1]] [[28:343|AWH 25-1]] [[28:368|AWH 26-1]] [[28:402|AWH 27-1]] [[28:470|AWH 28-1]]. The AIM names three of them as the types available to pilots: observations, analysis and forecasts [[34:62|AIM 7-1-3]].

callout.text: Application: have the learner name the type of every product before decoding it. An observation is a fact with an age [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]; a forecast carries uncertainty that grows the further out it goes [[28:25|AWH 3-2]].

The PTS still names some charts the 2026 AWH does not describe. The AIM itself says the termination of some legacy textual and graphical products may create confusion, and that decisions must use all available pertinent products [[34:62|AIM 7-1-3]]. This lesson flags each one and teaches the current product.

check.q: A learner asks why it matters whether a product is an observation or a forecast. What do you answer?
check.a: Observations are measured data that have an age (latency) [[34:62|AIM 7-1-3]] [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]; forecasts are predictions whose uncertainty grows with time [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]. The type tells her how much weight and how much margin to give it.

chunks.title: AWOS, ASOS and ATIS: what each one can and cannot tell you

body.p: **AWOS, ASOS, and ATIS reports.** ASOS is a joint NWS, FAA and DOD program and the nation's primary surface observing network. It sends hourly and special observations and broadcasts computer voice to aircraft near the airport [[28:286|AWH 24-2]]. AWOS is similar but generally reports fewer elements and may not have the same backup sensors or maintenance response [[28:287|AWH 24-3]]. An AWOS makes a METAR every 20 minutes and does not report SPECIs [[28:288|AWH 24-4]].

Clouds above 12,000 ft are not reported; CLR means no layers detected at or below 12,000 ft [[28:300|AWH 24-16]]

The system level is published in the Chart Supplement [[34:85|AIM 7-1-10]]

body.p: Timing traps worth teaching. In an automated report the sky condition is a 30-minute evaluation, and other elements are within 10 minutes of the observation time [[28:286|AWH 24-2]]. The one-minute observations on the radio are averaged too, and report worsening conditions faster than improving ones [[28:287|AWH 24-3]]. The broadcast wind can be up to 3 minutes old [[28:25|AWH 3-2]]. The ASOS broadcast can differ from the METAR on the internet or FIS-B, because the broadcast is the one-minute data [[28:287|AWH 24-3]].

Wind reference: network distribution such as Flight Service, the internet and FIS-B uses true degrees; local radio and telephone use magnetic [[28:287|AWH 24-3]]. Range: an ASOS/AWOS broadcast is typically receivable to 25 NM [[28:30|AWH 3-7]], engineered to 25 NM and 10,000 ft AGL [[34:88|AIM 7-1-10]]. ATIS may leave out the ceiling, sky condition, visibility and obstructions when the ceiling is above 5,000 ft and visibility more than 5 miles [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13]].

callout.text: AUTO limits: a station with no human augmentation cannot report freezing rain or freezing drizzle together with other precipitation, so near freezing with snow or mist reported, be alert for severe icing [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1f]]. AO1 means no precipitation discriminator; AO2 has one [[28:304|AWH 24-20]].

Application: put a local AWOS-3, an ASOS and an ATIS side by side and have the learner list what each one cannot tell her. Then look up the AWOS level in the Chart Supplement together [[34:85|AIM 7-1-10]].

check.q: Your learner plans an approach to a field with an AWOS. What should she understand about how fast a change will show up?
check.a: An AWOS makes a METAR every 20 minutes and no SPECIs, and its one-minute broadcast averages clouds over 30 minutes and visibility over 10 [[28:288|AWH 24-4]]. Listen to the broadcast close in, and expect improvement to show slowly.

chunks.title: Sources of weather data and the briefing

body.p: **Sources of weather data for flight planning.** The aviation weather program is a joint effort of NOAA, the FAA, the DOD, NASA and commercial providers [[28:18|AWH 2-1]]. The FAA establishes all requirements for aviation weather reports and forecasts [[28:21|AWH 2-4]].

head: Source
What it gives an IFR pilot
rows: NWS Aviation Weather Center (AWC)
AIRMETs, SIGMETs, Convective SIGMETs, and icing, turbulence and convective forecasts [[28:20|AWH 2-3]]; aviationweather.gov and the GFA Tool [[28:29|AWH 3-6]]
NWS Weather Prediction Center (WPC)
Surface pressure and frontal analyses [[28:20|AWH 2-3]]; surface analysis charts and short-range surface progs [[28:349|AWH 25-7]] [[28:449|AWH 27-48]]
NWS Storm Prediction Center (SPC)
Tornado and severe weather watches and hazardous weather forecasts [[28:20|AWH 2-3]], including the Convective Outlook [[28:457|AWH 27-56]]
NWS Weather Forecast Offices (WFO)
TAFs and Aviation Forecast Discussions [[28:21|AWH 2-4]]
Center Weather Service Units (CWSU)
NWS meteorologists at the ARTCCs who issue CWAs and Meteorological Impact Statements [[28:21|AWH 2-4]]
Flight Service
Briefings, flight planning and in-flight services at 1-800-WX-BRIEF [[28:22|AWH 2-5]]; online briefings, filing and alerts at 1800wxbrief.com [[28:28|AWH 3-5]]
ATC
Controllers advise of hazardous weather within 150 NM of their sector and may ask for PIREPs [[28:22|AWH 2-5]]
Commercial providers and EFBs
Mostly repackaged NWS data, but some products may differ substantially [[28:22|AWH 2-5]] [[28:23|AWH 2-6]]; they may not meet FAA/NWS quality control standards [[34:62|AIM 7-1-3]]

body.p: The AIM lists the approved sources as the Federal Government, EWINS and commercial weather information providers [[34:63|AIM 7-1-3]]. The FAA does not certify internet providers of aviation weather [[28:24|AWH 3-1]]. Pilots may get a regulatory compliant briefing without contacting Flight Service, and Flight Service briefings, online or voice, are time-stamped and archived for 45 days [[28:26|AWH 3-3]]. Briefers translate and interpret forecasts but may not make original forecasts [[28:28|AWH 3-5]].

**The briefing as your teaching skeleton.** A standard briefing runs: adverse conditions, VFR flight not recommended (VFR only), synopsis, current conditions, en route forecast, destination forecast, winds and temperatures aloft, then NOTAMs, ATC delays and other information [[28:26|AWH 3-3]] [[28:27|AWH 3-4]]. Current conditions are left out when departure is more than 2 hours away unless requested, and the destination forecast includes significant changes from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA [[28:27|AWH 3-4]]. An outlook briefing fits a departure 6 or more hours away; an abbreviated briefing updates an earlier one [[28:27|AWH 3-4]].

callout.text: Application: teach the learner to self-brief in the standard order, out loud, before she ever calls Flight Service. The AWH encourages a self-brief before calling [[28:26|AWH 3-3]], and the same order becomes the structure of every go/no-go debrief you give.

Tools can disagree. The NDFD may give different forecast information than the GFA for the same place and time [[28:29|AWH 3-6]]. When FIS data and voice information differ, use the most recent data from the most authoritative source [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]].

check.q: Your learner gets all her weather from one commercial app. Is that a legal briefing, and what do you want her to understand?
check.a: A regulatory compliant briefing does not require Flight Service [[28:26|AWH 3-3]], but the FAA does not certify internet providers [[28:24|AWH 3-1]] and non-government products may not meet FAA/NWS quality control [[34:62|AIM 7-1-3]]. She should know which products the app changes and cross-check the official ones.

chunks.title: METAR and SPECI: decoding the handbook's example

body.p: **METAR, TAF, and Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA)** begin with the METAR. Most briefing services decode it, but pilots still need to decode it in case the source does not [[28:289|AWH 24-5]]. The AWH builds its whole METAR section on one example:

Routine report for station KOKC (in the CONUS, K plus the three-letter identifier), 1st of the month at 1955 UTC, sent as the 2000 report [[28:292|AWH 24-8]] [[28:293|AWH 24-9]]
AUTO
Fully automated, no human oversight [[28:293|AWH 24-9]]
Wind 220° true at 15 kt, gusts 25 kt; direction varying from 180° to 250° [[28:294|AWH 24-10]]
Visibility 3/4 statute mile; runway 17L visual range 2,600 ft [[28:295|AWH 24-11]]
+TSRA BR
Thunderstorm with heavy rain; mist [[28:299|AWH 24-15]] [[28:296|AWH 24-12]]
OVC010CB
Overcast layer of cumulonimbus at 1,000 ft AGL: the ceiling [[28:300|AWH 24-16]] [[28:301|AWH 24-17]]
Temperature 18 °C, dewpoint 16 °C; altimeter 29.92 inHg [[28:302|AWH 24-18]]
RMK AO2 TSB25 TS OHD MOV E SLP132

Station with a precipitation discriminator; thunderstorm began at 25 past the hour; thunderstorm location remark, moving toward the east; sea level pressure 1013.2 mb [[28:304|AWH 24-20]] [[28:303|AWH 24-19]] [[28:306|AWH 24-22]] [[28:308|AWH 24-24]]

body.p: Now turn the decode into a decision. Visibility below 1 mile makes this LIFR even though the ceiling alone would be MVFR [[34:79|AIM 7-1-7]]. RVR is reported because visibility is 1 SM or less [[28:295|AWH 24-11]]. Thunderstorms imply possible severe or greater turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear [[28:438|AWH 27-37]].

**SPECI.** A SPECI is an unscheduled report made between hourly reports when criteria are met, and it has all the METAR elements [[28:290|AWH 24-6]]. IFR triggers include visibility crossing 3, 2, 1, 1/2 or 1/4 mile or the lowest standard approach minimum, the ceiling crossing 3,000, 1,500, 1,000 or 500 ft or the lowest approach minimum, and a thunderstorm beginning or ending [[28:290|AWH 24-6]].

callout.text: Application: decode in three passes. First the learner reads each group aloud by rote; second she explains what each group means for an approach; third she ties it to the TAF and the flight category. The AIH calls correlation the level aviation instruction should aim for [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

check.q: Your learner decodes this METAR perfectly but calls it "IFR, ceiling 1,000." What did she miss?
check.a: Flight category goes by the worse of ceiling and visibility. Visibility 3/4 SM is less than 1 mile, which is LIFR [[34:79|AIM 7-1-7]]; the 1,000 ft overcast alone would only be MVFR.

chunks.title: TAF: reading the destination and alternate windows

body.p: A TAF forecasts conditions within 5 SM of the center of the runway complex, uses the METAR weather codes and has no temperature [[28:407|AWH 27-6]]. Scheduled TAFs come out four times a day at 0000, 0600, 1200 and 1800Z, and a TAF AMD supersedes the previous TAF at once [[28:409|AWH 27-8]]. The AWH example from Pierre, South Dakota:

From 1500Z, a complete new forecast that replaces everything before it [[28:416|AWH 27-15]]

How does it compare with the alternate rules?

body.p: For IFR the learner reads the TAF twice. At the destination she looks from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA: no alternate is needed only if the destination has a standard instrument approach and the ceiling is forecast at least 2,000 ft above airport elevation and the visibility at least 3 SM [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)(1)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)(2)(i)]]. At the alternate she checks the forecast at her ETA there [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(c)]] against the procedure's alternate minimums, or, if none are published, 600 ft and 2 SM for a precision approach or 800 ft and 2 SM for a nonprecision approach [[60:470|14 CFR 91.169(c)(1)(i)]]. The Instrument lesson IR.I.B covers the alternate rules in detail.

callout.text: The TAF covers only 5 SM around the airport [[28:407|AWH 27-6]]. CB is the only cloud type in a TAF, and LLWS is always assumed in convective activity, even with no WS group [[28:415|AWH 27-14]].

Application: the sources do not say how TEMPO and PROB30 groups count for the alternate rules (see the gaps). Have the learner plan for the worst group in the window, and tell her plainly that this is your policy, not a regulation.

check.q: Your learner reads "FM120000 14012KT P6SM BKN080 OVC150" and says the earlier TEMPO mist still applies. What do you correct?
check.a: An FM group is a complete, self-contained forecast that supersedes everything before it [[28:416|AWH 27-15]]. That TEMPO also ended at 1400Z on the 11th [[28:419|AWH 27-18]].

chunks.title: The GFA and the static surface and clouds forecasts

body.p: The GFA website shows observations, forecasts and warnings from 14 hours in the past to 15 hours ahead: thunderstorms, clouds, flight category, precipitation, icing, turbulence and wind. Wind, icing and turbulence come in 3,000 ft steps from the surface to 30,000 ft MSL, and turbulence is split into low (below 18,000 ft MSL) and high graphics [[34:63|AIM 7-1-4]]. Its forecast tabs include the TAF, ceiling and visibility, clouds, precipitation, thunderstorms, winds, turbulence and ice; its observation tabs include METARs, PIREPs and radar and satellite [[34:63|AIM 7-1-4]] [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4]].

The GFA took over from the area forecast. The AIM describes its products as designed to replace the legacy FA [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4]], and the AWH says text FAs for the CONUS, Hawaii, the Gulf of America and the Caribbean have been retired; only Alaska keeps them [[28:425|AWH 27-24]]. The IFH's sample IFR trip still checks an area forecast [[23:319|IFH 10-28]], so tell learners who study from it that the GFA now fills that role.

For poor connections there are two static images. The Aviation Surface Forecast shows visibility, weather and winds with AIRMET Sierra for IFR and AIRMET Tango for strong surface winds. The Aviation Clouds Forecast shows coverage, bases, layers and tops in hundreds of feet MSL with AIRMETs for icing and mountain obscuration. Both update every 3 hours with snapshots 3 to 18 hours ahead [[28:423|AWH 27-22]].

callout.text: Layers can hide hazards. Users can turn off functions such as the AIRMET and SIGMET overlays, which can hide hazardous weather on the flightpath [[28:471|AWH 28-2]].
Application: have the learner set up the GFA for her route, then ask her to show you every layer she turned off and why. It catches the hidden-overlay trap before it becomes a habit.

check.q: A learner studying the IFH asks where to find the area forecast for her route in Ohio. What do you tell her?
check.a: Text area forecasts for the CONUS were retired and replaced by the GFA Tool and the Aviation Surface and Clouds Forecasts [[28:425|AWH 27-24]] [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4]].

chunks.title: Surface analysis, weather depiction and radar summary charts

body.p: **Surface analysis, weather depiction, and radar summary charts.** The PTS lists three charts. Only the first is still described in the 2026 Aviation Weather Handbook.

**Surface analysis chart.** An analyzed chart of surface observations: sea level pressure isobars, highs, lows, ridges, troughs, fronts and boundaries such as drylines and outflow boundaries. The WPC issues it eight times a day, valid at 00, 03, 06, 09, 12, 15, 18 and 21 UTC, and also combines it with radar or satellite imagery [[28:350|AWH 25-8]]. The symbols on a front point toward where it is moving [[28:348|AWH 25-6]]. Station plots give the ceiling in hundreds of feet AGL and the visibility in whole statute miles [[28:356|AWH 25-14]].

**Weather depiction chart.** The PHAK still describes it: surface conditions from METARs, sent every 3 hours, with IFR areas hatched and MVFR areas outlined [[1:325|PHAK 13-15]]. The 2026 AWH does not describe it; its list of analyses is surface charts, upper air, freezing level, CIP, GTG and RTMA [[28:343|AWH 25-1]]. What the AWH teaches instead is the flight category display: color-coded METAR and sometimes TAF station plots, LIFR purple, IFR red, MVFR blue and VFR green, meant for situational awareness only [[28:50|AWH 3-27]] [[28:51|AWH 3-28]]. The GFA adds ceiling and visibility tabs [[34:63|AIM 7-1-4]] [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4]].

**Radar summary chart.** The AIM still mentions national radar summary charts made from radar reports [[34:93|AIM 7-1-11]], and the PHAK glossary defines one [[1:500|PHAK G-24]]. The AWH does not describe the chart; its radar section covers NEXRAD mosaics, Composite Reflectivity, Base Reflectivity and Echo Tops [[28:325|AWH 24-41]].

head: What to teach
Current radar fact
rows: Composite or base

Composite Reflectivity shows the strongest return in the column; Base Reflectivity is only the lowest tilt, so precipitation can be heavier than it shows [[28:325|AWH 24-41]] [[28:326|AWH 24-42]] [[28:327|AWH 24-43]]
Cockpit NEXRAD
Avionics mosaics use Composite Reflectivity [[28:325|AWH 24-41]]; datalinked mosaics show where precipitation was and may be 15 to 20 minutes older than shown [[28:327|AWH 24-43]]
Intensity words
Light below 26 dBZ, moderate 26 to 40, heavy over 40 to 50, extreme 50 and up [[28:324|AWH 24-40]]
Echo tops
Height of the 18 dBZ echo; cloud tops are higher [[28:327|AWH 24-43]]
Blind spots
Radar does not detect clouds or fog; a clear display does not mean no significant weather [[34:93|AIM 7-1-11]]

callout.text: Say it plainly on the checkride: the PTS names the weather depiction and radar summary charts, the current AWH does not describe them, and you teach flight category displays, the GFA and NEXRAD products instead. The AIM itself notes that some legacy products have been terminated [[34:62|AIM 7-1-3]]. No source here gives the date either chart ended (see the gaps).

check.q: An examiner asks you to teach the radar summary chart. How do you answer?
check.a: Explain what it was, a graphic summary of radar weather reports [[1:500|PHAK G-24]], say that the current AWH teaches NEXRAD mosaics, composite and base reflectivity and echo tops instead [[28:325|AWH 24-41]], then teach those, including their age and limits [[28:327|AWH 24-43]].

body.p: **Significant weather prognostic charts.** The Low-Level SIGWX charts give an overview of selected hazards up to FL240 at 12 and 24 hours ahead over the CONUS and coastal waters, each a snapshot at its valid time [[28:436|AWH 27-35]]. The AWC issues them four times a day. They show flight categories, turbulence and freezing levels; in-flight icing is not shown [[28:437|AWH 27-36]].

bullets: IFR areas: solid red line. MVFR areas: scalloped blue line. VFR areas are not drawn [[28:438|AWH 27-37]].
Moderate or greater turbulence: bold dashed lines. 240/100 means from FL240 down to 10,000 ft MSL; 080/ means from the surface to 8,000 ft MSL [[28:438|AWH 27-37]] [[28:439|AWH 27-38]].
Turbulence from thunderstorms is not drawn [[28:439|AWH 27-38]]; the legend reminds that thunderstorms imply possible severe or greater turbulence, severe icing and LLWS [[28:438|AWH 27-37]].
Colors are not standard and vary by website [[28:436|AWH 27-35]].

body.p: **Surface prog charts.** The WPC's short-range surface progs forecast pressure systems, fronts and precipitation over several days, combining WPC fronts and isobars with NDFD forecasts [[28:449|AWH 27-48]]. Shading shows chance (25 to under 55 percent) and likely (55 percent or more) areas of rain, snow, mixed precipitation, freezing rain and thunderstorms [[28:450|AWH 27-49]]. Some websites pair the SIGWX and surface progs as a four-panel view [[28:437|AWH 27-36]]; the PHAK describes the 2015 change from the old four-panel chart to a two-panel chart plus an enhanced surface chart [[1:326|PHAK 13-16]].

callout.text: Application: use the prog at the outlook stage to ask "Is this trip likely to work?" and the TAFs later to ask "Will it work at my ETA?" The chart's own legend says flight planning only and points to the TAFs for terminal forecasts [[28:438|AWH 27-37]].

check.q: Your learner uses the 12-hour Low-Level SIGWX chart to check her route for icing. What is wrong?
check.a: In-flight icing is not shown on the Low-Level SIGWX chart [[28:437|AWH 27-36]]. She needs AIRMET Zulu [[28:383|AWH 26-16]], the icing forecasts and the PIREPs.

chunks.title: Winds and temperatures aloft, and freezing level charts

body.p: **Winds and temperatures aloft charts.** The FB code is DDff+TT: direction true in tens of degrees, speed in knots, temperature in °C. 9900 means light and variable. Speeds of 100 to 199 kt add 50 to the direction, so 7545 is 250° at 145 kt. No wind is forecast within 1,500 ft of the station elevation and no temperature within 2,500 ft, and above 24,000 ft the minus sign is dropped [[28:405|AWH 27-4]]. The AWH sample line for Kansas City:

head: Altitude
Code
Decoded
rows: Light and variable; no temperature forecast [[28:406|AWH 27-5]]

body.p: The AWH calls the FB product archaic: updated only four times a day, one value for long time blocks, at points 100 to 150 miles apart, while models such as the Rapid Refresh update every hour [[28:404|AWH 27-3]] [[28:405|AWH 27-4]]. Graphical FB displays vary by website [[28:407|AWH 27-6]], and the GFA shows winds by altitude [[34:63|AIM 7-1-4]].

**Freezing level charts.** The freezing level is the lowest altitude over a location at which the air reaches 0 °C. The freezing level analysis and forecast graphics are updated hourly; colors give the lowest freezing level in hundreds of feet MSL, white means the whole column is below freezing, and hatched or spotted areas mean a below-freezing surface with multiple freezing levels aloft [[28:365|AWH 25-23]] [[28:454|AWH 27-53]]. They supplement the freezing level information in the icing AIRMETs [[28:454|AWH 27-53]]. On the Low-Level SIGWX chart, freezing levels aloft are dashed lines every 4,000 ft MSL and the surface freezing level is a saw-toothed line [[28:439|AWH 27-38]].

Other freezing level clues: the FB temperatures give the approximate freezing level [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1g]], near 9,000 ft in the sample above, and AIRMET Zulu gives freezing level heights [[28:383|AWH 26-16]].

callout.text: Why it matters: pilots need the freezing levels, and any inversions or multiple freezing levels, to decide how to exit icing if they meet it [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1c]]. The warmer altitude may not be a lower one [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]].

check.q: The chart shows the 040 and 080 freezing level lines with your learner's destination midway between them. What freezing level does she use?
check.a: Interpolate: midway between the 4,000 and 8,000 ft lines is about 6,000 ft MSL [[28:439|AWH 27-38]].

chunks.title: PIREPs: the only report from inside the cloud

body.p: **PIREPS.** Every PIREP has the message type, location, time, altitude, aircraft type and at least one weather element. Altitudes are MSL, visibility is in statute miles, other distances in nautical miles and time in UTC [[28:310|AWH 24-26]]. Urgent (UUA) reports cover tornadoes and funnel clouds, severe or extreme turbulence, severe icing, hail, LLWS within 2,000 ft of the surface, volcanic ash and anything else the receiver judges hazardous [[28:311|AWH 24-27]].

head: Group
Decoded
rows: UA /OV APE230010
Routine report; 230° at 10 NM from the Appleton VOR [[28:311|AWH 24-27]]
/TM 1516 /FL085 /TP BE20
1516 UTC, 8,500 ft MSL, Super King Air 200 [[28:312|AWH 24-28]]
/SK BKN040-TOP065
Base of a broken layer 4,000 ft MSL, top 6,500 ft MSL [[28:313|AWH 24-29]]
/WX FV03SM BR /TA M02
Flight visibility 3 SM in mist; air temperature -2 °C [[28:313|AWH 24-29]] [[28:314|AWH 24-30]]
/WV 23008KT /TB LGT
Wind 230° magnetic at 8 kt; light turbulence [[28:314|AWH 24-30]] [[28:315|AWH 24-31]]
/IC TRACE RIME /RM TCU W
Trace rime icing; remark, towering cumulus to the west [[28:315|AWH 24-31]] [[28:301|AWH 24-17]] [[28:317|AWH 24-33]]

body.p: Use the example to practice questioning. The /IC group carries no altitude, so by the format it applies at 8,500 ft [[28:315|AWH 24-31]], yet the layer top was 6,500 ft. Was the ice picked up in the climb? A full report would say so in the remarks, for example DURC [[28:312|AWH 24-28]] [[28:317|AWH 24-33]].

bullets: PIREPs are generally the most useful icing information, because they are factual reports for specific times and places [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1]].
No recent icing PIREP does not mean no ice; icing varies greatly in space and time [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3a]].
A Boeing 747 may report light icing where a Mooney would meet severe icing; reports depend on the airplane and the pilot [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3b]].

ATC must ask for PIREPs when ceilings at or below 5,000 ft, visibility at or below 5 miles, thunderstorms, light or greater icing, moderate or greater turbulence, wind shear or volcanic ash are reported or forecast [[34:101|AIM 7-1-18]].

callout.text: Under IFR in controlled airspace the pilot in command must report any unforecast weather encountered [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183(b)]]. Teach learners to report good weather as well as bad [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5]].

check.q: Your learner finds no icing PIREPs on her route under an AIRMET Zulu and says that proves the AIRMET is wrong. How do you respond?
check.a: No recent PIREP may only mean no one flew there, or no one reported; icing varies greatly in space and time [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3a]]. The forecast stands until reports show otherwise.

chunks.title: Inflight weather advisories: the system and how it reaches you

body.p: **Inflight weather advisories.** These are forecasts that advise en route aircraft of potentially hazardous weather; over the conterminous U.S. the AWC and 20 CWSUs issue them [[34:68|AIM 7-1-6]]. There are four types: the SIGMET, the Convective SIGMET, the AIRMET and the CWA. Heights are MSL except ceilings (CIG), which are AGL [[34:69|AIM 7-1-6]].

**Center Weather Advisory (CWA).** A CWSU product for weather that meets or approaches advisory criteria when no AWC advisory is in effect, or to expand or upgrade one that is [[28:387|AWH 26-20]] [[28:388|AWH 26-21]]. A CWA is valid for up to 2 hours [[28:388|AWH 26-21]]. Because of its short lead time it is not a flight planning product; it is a nowcast for conditions beginning within the next 2 hours [[34:78|AIM 7-1-6]]. In the AIM example, ZKC3 CWA 032140 / ZKC CWA 301 VALID UNTIL 032340 / ISOLD SVR TSTM over KCOU MOVG SWWD 10 KTS is Kansas City Center's third phenomenon of the day, first issuance, valid until 2340Z [[34:79|AIM 7-1-6]].

**How advisories reach the cockpit.** An ARTCC broadcasts an alert once on all frequencies for a Convective SIGMET, SIGMET, AIRMET (except in the contiguous U.S.), urgent PIREP or CWA within 150 miles of its airspace, and tells pilots to contact Flight Service for details [[34:79|AIM 7-1-8]]. Tower and approach positions may limit this to 50 miles [[34:80|AIM 7-1-8]]. Over the CONUS, AIRMETs are available from Flight Service and on FIS-B [[34:73|AIM 7-1-6]]. Severe weather watch bulletins and their alert messages supplement the advisories [[34:69|AIM 7-1-6]]; they are covered with the outlook below.

callout.text: Cockpit weather is strategic. FIS products such as datalinked radar support decisions 20 minutes or more ahead, not tactical avoidance under 3 minutes, and never replace a preflight briefing [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]]. NEXRAD is for broad strategic avoidance of thunderstorms, never for navigating through them [[28:25|AWH 3-2]].

Application: in the simulator or on a long IFR flight, read a CWA or advisory alert to the learner as ATC would, and have her decide on the spot: continue, ask for a deviation, or divert. This is the in-flight half of go/no-go.

check.q: Why shouldn't your learner build her preflight plan around a CWA?
check.a: A CWA is a short-lead nowcast for conditions in the next 2 hours, not a flight planning product [[34:78|AIM 7-1-6]]. She plans with the forecasts, AIRMETs, SIGMETs and PIREPs, and uses CWAs to update in flight.

body.p: **SIGMETs and AIRMETs.** Know the criteria cold: they tell the learner which hazard each advisory covers and how strong it is.

head: Advisory
Issued for
Timing and details
rows: SIGMET (CONUS, non-convective)
Severe or greater turbulence, severe icing, widespread dust storm or sandstorm, volcanic ash [[28:372|AWH 26-5]]

Unscheduled, valid up to 4 hours [[28:372|AWH 26-5]]; the AIM gives 6 hours for volcanic ash and tropical cyclones [[34:69|AIM 7-1-6]]; named November through Yankee, without Sierra and Tango [[28:371|AWH 26-4]]
Convective SIGMET

Severe thunderstorms (surface winds 50 kt or more, hail 3/4 inch or more, tornadoes), embedded thunderstorms, a line of thunderstorms, heavy precipitation over 40 percent or more of at least 3,000 square miles [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]
Hourly at H+55 for the eastern, central and western regions; each forecast valid up to 1 hour; "CONVECTIVE SIGMET... NONE" when nothing meets criteria [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]
AIRMET (graphical over the CONUS)

IFR (ceiling under 1,000 ft and/or visibility under 3 miles), widespread mountain obscuration, moderate icing, freezing levels, moderate turbulence, LLWS potential below 2,000 ft AGL, sustained surface winds over 30 kt [[34:73|AIM 7-1-6]]
Every 6 hours; snapshots no more than 3 hours apart out to 12 hours [[34:73|AIM 7-1-6]]

callout.text: Sierra: IFR and mountain obscuration. Tango: moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 kt or more, LLWS. Zulu: moderate icing and freezing levels [[28:383|AWH 26-16]].

body.p: Any Convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]. Its polygon is a snapshot at 55 past the hour; fast-moving areas will likely move out of it within the hour, so compare the graphic with the text and use it for strategic planning only [[28:374|AWH 26-7]].

Decoding the AWH example: issued on the 22nd at 1855Z, the 20th central-region Convective SIGMET of the day, valid until 2055Z, North and South Dakota, from 90 NM west of Minot to Grand Forks to Aberdeen and back. An intensifying area of severe thunderstorms is moving from 240° at 45 kt with tops above FL450; gusts to 60 kt were reported, and tornadoes, 2 inch hail and 65 kt gusts are possible in North Dakota [[28:377|AWH 26-10]]. Note that the AWH gives Convective SIGMETs a 2-hour validity [[28:375|AWH 26-8]], while the newer AIM page says each forecast is valid up to 1 hour [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]; see the instructor notes.

G-AIRMET timing rule: if the 00-hour snapshot shows nothing, the 03-hour shows a hazard and the 06-hour shows nothing, assume the hazard from 0001 to 0559 [[34:74|AIM 7-1-6]]. A graphic of a SIGMET area is not the entire SIGMET; read the text too [[28:369|AWH 26-2]].

callout.text: Do not rely on advisories alone. Icing AIRMETs are not issued unless the affected area is large, and a severe icing PIREP will not automatically produce an icing SIGMET [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1d]].

check.q: Your learner says, "No SIGMET, so no severe icing." What do you teach?
check.a: A severe icing PIREP does not automatically produce a SIGMET, and icing AIRMETs need a large area [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1d]]. She has to read the PIREPs [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1e]].

chunks.title: Severe weather outlook charts and watches

body.p: **Severe weather outlook charts.** The IFH lists the "Severe Weather Outlook (AC)" among the products for planning around turbulence [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. The 2026 AWH describes the SPC product with the same AC identifier as the Convective Outlook (AC) [[28:457|AWH 27-56]]. That is the product to teach.

The Convective Outlook shows the potential for severe convection (a tornado, wind gusts of 50 kt or more, or hail 1 inch or more) and for general thunderstorms over the next eight days. Severe risk is marginal (MRGL), slight (SLGT), enhanced (ENH), moderate (MDT) or high (HIGH), and days 1 to 3 also show general thunderstorm (TSTM) areas [[28:457|AWH 27-56]].

**Watches.** The SPC issues the Aviation Watch Notification Message (SAW), formerly the Alert Severe Weather Watch Bulletin (AWW), and public severe thunderstorm and tornado watch messages, formerly the Severe Weather Watch Bulletins (WW). A watch means severe weather is possible during the watch; a warning means it has been observed or is expected within the hour. The SAW only approximates the watch area [[28:461|AWH 27-60]].

Two more convection planning products: the TCF, a high-confidence convection forecast every two hours valid at 4, 6 and 8 hours, and the ECFP, the probability of thunderstorms through 72 hours [[28:458|AWH 27-57]] [[28:460|AWH 27-59]]. The ECFP is mainly intended for air traffic managers [[28:38|AWH 3-15]].

callout.text: Application: in thunderstorm season, open every IFR planning lesson with the Day 1 and Day 2 outlooks. If the route sits in SLGT or higher, have the learner build the plan around the convection before anything else. A solid line of thunderstorms is one of the hazards the AIH calls almost always "red" [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

check.q: The Day 2 outlook shows MRGL over the destination. Your learner says, "Marginal means no storms." What do you correct?
check.a: MRGL is the lowest of the five severe risk categories, but it is still a severe risk area; general thunderstorms are shown separately as TSTM [[28:457|AWH 27-56]]. She should follow the outlook and forecasts as the day nears.

chunks.title: Teaching the IFR go/no-go weather briefing

body.p: The goal is correlation: the learner ties each product to the others and to this airplane, this route and herself [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]. Build it in blocks, then hand her the decision. When teaching decision making, turn the planning over to the learner as soon as possible and act as a mentor [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

head: Stage
What the learner does
What you do
rows: 1. Rote
Decodes the AWH sample METAR, TAF, FB line and PIREP aloud [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Correct the code; no decisions yet
2. Understanding
Explains what each item means for an IFR flight, such as a ceiling versus vertical visibility, or LIFR versus IFR [[28:300|AWH 24-16]] [[34:79|AIM 7-1-7]]
Ask "so what?" after every group
3. Application
Self-briefs a real route in the standard briefing order [[28:26|AWH 3-3]] [[28:27|AWH 3-4]]
Review it as you would any preflight calculation [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]
4. Correlation
Lays each hazard on the route by time and altitude and checks it against the airplane, the alternate rules and her written personal minimums [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]] [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]
Ask questions, let her decide, then have her lead the debrief [[25:145|AIH 7-1]]

body.p: A go/no-go flow you can teach, built on the sources:

bullets: Days ahead: the Convective Outlook and the progs for the big picture [[28:457|AWH 27-56]] [[28:449|AWH 27-48]], and an outlook briefing 6 or more hours out [[28:27|AWH 3-4]]. Risk management begins days or weeks before a flight [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].
Adverse conditions first: SIGMETs, Convective SIGMETs, AIRMETs and CWAs, and icing if the airplane is not certified for it [[28:26|AWH 3-3]].
Synopsis: the surface analysis for fronts and pressure systems [[28:350|AWH 25-8]]; a front's location, type and movement matter for icing [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1a]].
Current: METARs and flight categories, radar with its age, and PIREPs for tops and ice [[28:51|AWH 3-28]] [[28:327|AWH 24-43]] [[28:313|AWH 24-29]].
Forecast: the GFA, the destination TAF 1 hour either side of ETA, and the alternate TAF at its ETA [[34:63|AIM 7-1-4]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(c)]].
Aloft: winds, temperatures and freezing levels, and the way out if ice is met: altitude, heading, airspeed or an alternate airport [[28:405|AWH 27-4]] [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1m]].
Decide against written personal minimums, and never adjust them to complete a specific flight [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

head: Learner error
What it looks like
How you correct it
rows: Ignoring product age
Treats a datalinked radar image as live
Show that mosaics may be 15 to 20 minutes older than shown [[28:327|AWH 24-43]], and teach strategic use only [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]]
Reading silence as safety
No PIREPs or no SIGMET, so no ice
Review the PIREP cautions and the SIGMET gap [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3a]] [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1d]]
Hidden layers
GFA set up with the AIRMET overlay off
Have her show every layer she turned off [[28:471|AWH 28-2]]
Destination only
Checks the TAF at ETA, not the window or the alternate
Trusting a low FRAT score
Low score despite one big hazard such as embedded thunderstorms
One extreme risk can hide in a low score [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]

body.p: Analyze before you correct. A mistake is an error of thought, often from a gap or misconception, while a slip is an error of action [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]; having the learner think aloud through the briefing shows you which one you are looking at. Instrument training should cover the risk of flight in low IMC, in icing conditions or above the freezing level [[25:189|AIH 10-5]].

callout.text: Before an IFR flight the pilot in command must become familiar with the weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives available if the flight cannot be completed, and any known ATC delays [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]].

check.q: How do you know your learner has reached the correlation level with weather?
check.a: She links the products to each other and to the flight without prompting, for example turning an AIRMET Zulu, the freezing level and a PIREP of tops into an exit plan [[25:66|AIH 3-15]] [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1m]].

scenario.title: A February IFR trip in a single not approved for icing
scenario.setup: Your instrument learner is two weeks from her checkride. She wants to fly a 180 NM IFR trip tomorrow afternoon in the school's fixed-gear single, which is not approved for flight in icing. Tonight her self-briefing shows a G-AIRMET Zulu for moderate icing from the freezing level to 10,000 ft over the middle of the route, a freezing level near 4,000 ft MSL, no icing PIREPs along the route, and a destination TAF of BKN015 OVC030 from 1 hour before to 1 hour after her ETA. The destination has an AWOS-3P. She has filed for 6,000 ft and plans no alternate.

questions.q: It is about 18 hours before departure. What kind of briefing does she have tonight, and what should she do tomorrow?
questions.a: With departure 6 or more hours away, this is outlook information for planning only; a standard or abbreviated briefing before departure is advisable [[28:27|AWH 3-4]] [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5]].

questions.q: She says the AIRMET Zulu must be overdone because nobody has reported ice. How do you respond?
questions.a: No recent PIREP may mean no one flew there or no one reported, and icing varies greatly in space and time [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3a]]. The forecast stands until reports show otherwise, and in an airplane not certified for icing her planning should emphasize ice avoidance [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1m]].

questions.q: At 6,000 ft she would be above the 4,000 ft freezing level in cloud inside the AIRMET area. What should she weigh for this airplane?
questions.a: A pilot of an airplane not certificated for icing should avoid all icing conditions [[23:94|IFH 4-17]], and inflight icing can reasonably be expected in clouds at or below 0 °C [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]]. Planning should emphasize ice avoidance and an alternate course of action [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1m]].

questions.q: Is she right that no alternate is needed?
questions.a: No. BKN015 is a 1,500 ft ceiling [[28:415|AWH 27-14]], below the 2,000 ft needed in the hour either side of ETA, so an alternate is required [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)(2)(i)]].

questions.q: How do you turn tonight into a lesson rather than simply telling her no?
questions.a: Ask questions and let her reach the decision, as the AIH example instructor does [[25:145|AIH 7-1]]. Have her name the hazard with PAVE and see that some weather hazards are almost always red, then choose a mitigation: delay, cancel or transfer the risk [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

questions.q: Next morning the destination AWOS reports AUTO, light snow and mist at 0 °C. What else should she consider?
questions.a: An unaugmented AUTO station cannot report freezing rain or drizzle together with other precipitation, so near freezing with snow or mist she should be alert for severe icing [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1f]] [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1k]]. An AWOS-3P has no freezing rain sensor at all; that comes only with AWOS-4 [[28:288|AWH 24-4]].

skills.do: Explain aloud, as you would to a learner, where IFR weather comes from: the NWS centers and offices, Flight Service, ATC, ASOS, AWOS and ATIS, FIS-B and commercial providers, with what each can and cannot tell the pilot.
skills.practice: Pick your home airport and a nearby AWOS field and brief a classmate on each source in under five minutes, including the AWOS level from the Chart Supplement [[34:85|AIM 7-1-10]] and why the ASOS broadcast can differ from the METAR [[28:287|AWH 24-3]].

skills.do: Teach a learner to decode and connect the reports and charts the Task lists, saying plainly which listed charts are legacy and what replaces them, and lead her through a complete IFR go/no-go self-briefing.
skills.practice: Use the AWH sample METAR, TAF, FB line, PIREP and Convective SIGMET [[28:291|AWH 24-7]] [[28:419|AWH 27-18]] [[28:406|AWH 27-5]] [[28:310|AWH 24-26]] [[28:377|AWH 26-10]], then live products for a real route, and run the learning levels from rote to correlation [[25:65|AIH 3-14]] [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

quiz.q: Your learner will rely on the AWOS-3 at her destination. Which statement about it is correct?
options: It sends a METAR every 20 minutes and no SPECIs
It sends a SPECI whenever visibility drops below 3 SM
It reports cloud layers up to 25,000 ft above the field
It reports freezing rain mixed with other precipitation
quiz.why: An AWOS makes a METAR every 20 minutes and does not report SPECIs; AWOS-3 adds cloud height and a rain gauge to AWOS-2, and freezing rain comes only with AWOS-4 [[28:288|AWH 24-4]].

quiz.q: The ATIS your learner copies says nothing about ceiling or visibility. What may she conclude?
options: The weather observer was not on duty
Ceiling and visibility are below approach minimums
Ceiling 5,000 ft or more, visibility 5 or more
The ceilometer has failed, so she has to ask the tower
quiz.why: The absence of sky condition or ceiling and visibility on ATIS indicates a ceiling of 5,000 ft or above and visibility of 5 miles or more [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13]].

quiz.q: Using the AWH sample METAR in the figure, what flight category is KOKC?
options: MVFR, since the ceiling is at 1,000 ft
IFR, because visibility is below 3 miles
VFR under the cloud, with a thunderstorm
LIFR, since visibility is below 1 mile
quiz.why: LIFR is a ceiling below 500 ft and/or visibility below 1 mile [[34:79|AIM 7-1-7]], and the report shows 3/4SM [[28:295|AWH 24-11]]. The 1,000 ft ceiling alone would be MVFR, which is the tempting wrong answer.

quiz.q: A learner reads WS020/35035KT in a TAF as "35 knots of wind shear." What does the group mean?
options: Shear from surface to 2,000 ft; wind there 350° at 35 kt
A 35 kt airspeed gain or loss expected below 2,000 ft AGL
Wind shear layer at 2,000 ft MSL with a 35 kt gust factor
Convective shear from storms forecast within 20 NM of field
quiz.why: WS020 is non-convective LLWS from the surface to 2,000 ft AGL, and 35035KT is the wind at the top of the layer, not the amount of shear [[28:416|AWH 27-15]]. Convective LLWS is assumed without any WS group [[28:415|AWH 27-14]].

quiz.q: Your learner, studying an older text, asks where the area forecast for her route went. What is the best answer?
options: It moved into the TAF remarks section
For the CONUS it was retired for the GFA
It is still issued, but only by telephone
It became part of the Convective Outlook
quiz.why: Text FAs for the CONUS have been retired and replaced by the GFA Tool and the Aviation Surface and Clouds Forecasts [[28:425|AWH 27-24]]; the AIM calls the GFA products designed to replace the legacy FA [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4]].

quiz.q: Which product will NOT show your learner forecast in-flight icing?
options: AIRMET Zulu
Forecast Icing Product
Low-Level SIGWX chart
GFA ice tab
quiz.why: In-flight icing is not depicted on the Low-Level SIGWX chart [[28:437|AWH 27-36]]. AIRMET Zulu covers moderate icing [[28:383|AWH 26-16]], the FIP forecasts icing [[28:454|AWH 27-53]] and the GFA has an ice tab [[34:64|AIM 7-1-4]].

quiz.q: In a PIREP, how should your learner read /SK OVC015-TOP035?
options: Overcast base 1,500 ft AGL, top 3,500 ft AGL
Overcast base 1,500 ft MSL, top 3,500 ft MSL
Overcast at 150 ft AGL, visibility 3,500 ft
Overcast tops 1,500 ft MSL, bases 3,500 ft MSL
quiz.why: PIREP bases and tops are in hundreds of feet MSL [[28:312|AWH 24-28]] [[28:313|AWH 24-29]]. METAR and TAF cloud heights, by contrast, are AGL [[28:300|AWH 24-16]], which is the usual mix-up.

quiz.q: Your learner says, "There's no SIGMET, so there's no severe icing on my route." What do you teach?
options: Right; a severe icing PIREP always triggers a SIGMET at once
Right, unless a Convective SIGMET is nearby
Wrong; only CWAs report icing, so check those
A severe icing PIREP may not make a SIGMET; read PIREPs
quiz.why: A severe icing PIREP will not automatically result in an icing SIGMET, and icing AIRMETs need a large area, so pilots should consult PIREPs [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1d]] [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1e]].

quiz.q: A G-AIRMET for icing shows nothing at 00 hours, a hazard area at 03 and nothing at 06. How should your learner treat it?
options: Assume the hazard from just after 00 to just before 06
Assume the hazard only at exactly the 03-hour time
Ignore it, since one snapshot is not a real forecast
Assume it for the hour from 0230 to 0330 only
quiz.why: The user should assume the hazard exists between the snapshots, from the 0001 hour to the 0559 hour in this example [[34:74|AIM 7-1-6]].

quiz.q: What does any Convective SIGMET imply, even when its text does not say so?
options: Hail of 2 inches or more at the surface
Severe turbulence, severe icing and LLWS
Tops above FL450 and a tornado watch
IFR conditions and mountain obscuration
quiz.why: Any Convective SIGMET implies severe or greater turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]] [[28:374|AWH 26-7]].

quiz.q: An examiner asks you to teach the weather depiction chart. Which answer best matches the current sources?
options: Refuse, since the chart is not legal for planning
Teach it from the AWH, which still describes it
Explain the PHAK chart, then teach category maps
Teach the Convective Outlook, which replaced it
quiz.why: The PHAK still describes the chart [[1:325|PHAK 13-15]], but the 2026 AWH's list of analyses has no weather depiction chart [[28:343|AWH 25-1]] and teaches flight category displays instead [[28:51|AWH 3-28]]. The Convective Outlook is a thunderstorm product, not its replacement [[28:457|AWH 27-56]].

quiz.q: The datalinked NEXRAD on your learner's tablet shows a gap between two cells ahead. What do you teach?
options: Use the gap; the picture refreshes every few seconds
Use the gap only if base reflectivity also shows it
The gap is safe as long as no lightning is shown
It shows where rain was, maybe 15 to 20 minutes ago
quiz.why: Datalinked mosaics show where the precipitation was and may be 15 to 20 minutes older than the age shown [[28:327|AWH 24-43]]; NEXRAD is for strategic avoidance and never for navigating through thunderstorms [[28:25|AWH 3-2]] [[34:81|AIM 7-1-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner calls Flight Service and asks the briefer to forecast whether the fog will lift by 1500Z. What should she expect?
options: Briefers interpret forecasts but make none of their own
Briefers issue amended TAFs on request for GA pilots
Briefers forecast only for airports without a TAF
Briefers forecast fog but not icing or storms
final_quiz.why: Flight Service specialists are not authorized to make original forecasts; they translate and interpret the available forecasts and reports [[28:28|AWH 3-5]] [[34:66|AIM 7-1-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants planning weather for a departure 8 hours away. Which briefing type does the AWH describe for that?
options: Abbreviated
Outlook
Standard
Inflight
final_quiz.why: An outlook briefing may be requested when departure is six or more hours away; a follow-up standard or abbreviated briefing before departure is advisable [[28:27|AWH 3-4]].

final_quiz.q: A TAF line reads TEMPO 2215/2217 30025G35KT 1 1/2SM SHRA BKN010. What does TEMPO tell your learner?
options: A 30 percent chance of these conditions
A permanent change starting at 1500Z
Brief changes over 50 percent likely
Conditions only in the 5 to 10 SM ring
final_quiz.why: TEMPO means temporary fluctuations with more than a 50 percent probability, each lasting an hour or less and covering less than half the period [[28:417|AWH 27-16]]. A 30 percent chance is PROB30 [[28:418|AWH 27-17]], and VC is never used in TEMPO groups [[28:414|AWH 27-13]].

final_quiz.q: Which TAF group starts a complete new forecast that replaces everything before it?
options: TEMPO
PROB30
BECMG
FM
final_quiz.why: The FM group is followed by a complete, self-contained description, and all conditions before it are superseded [[28:416|AWH 27-15]]. BECMG appears in the joint-use TAF format, not as an NWS change group [[28:418|AWH 27-17]].

final_quiz.q: The AWH sample FB line shows 1709+06 at 6,000 ft and 2018+00 at 9,000 ft. What should your learner take from it for icing?
options: The freezing level is near 9,000 ft
The freezing level is near 6,000 ft
There is no freezing level at all
The 9,000 ft wind is 090° at 20 kt
final_quiz.why: 2018+00 decodes as 200° at 18 kt and 0 °C at 9,000 ft [[28:406|AWH 27-5]], and FB temperatures give the approximate freezing level [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1g]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks how to tell which way a front is moving on the surface analysis. You answer:
options: Away from the side the symbols are on
Toward the side the symbols point
Always west to east with the jet stream
Along the isobars toward low pressure
final_quiz.why: The symbols on a front indicate its type and point in the direction toward which it is moving [[28:348|AWH 25-6]].

final_quiz.q: On a Low-Level SIGWX chart your learner sees 240/100 beside a turbulence area. What does it mean?
options: An area 240 NM long and 100 NM wide
From 2,400 ft up to 10,000 ft AGL
From FL240 down to 10,000 ft MSL
Wind 240° at 100 kt in that area
final_quiz.why: Turbulence height is two numbers separated by a solidus, top over base: 240/100 is from FL240 down to 10,000 ft MSL [[28:439|AWH 27-38]].

final_quiz.q: The Day 1 Convective Outlook shows your learner's route in a TSTM area only. What does TSTM mean?
options: A tornado watch is in effect there
Thunderstorms are certain in the period
Severe storms with large hail are likely
General, non-severe thunderstorm area
final_quiz.why: Days 1 to 3 of the Convective Outlook depict areas of general thunderstorms (TSTM) separately from the severe risk categories MRGL to HIGH [[28:457|AWH 27-56]]. Watches are separate SPC products [[28:461|AWH 27-60]].

final_quiz.q: What is the difference between a severe thunderstorm watch and a warning?
options: Watch: severe weather possible; warning: observed or expected
Watch is from WFOs; warning is from the Storm Prediction Center
Watch covers one county; warning covers an entire state
Watch is for pilots only; warning is for the public only
final_quiz.why: A watch means severe weather is possible; a warning means it has been observed or is expected within the hour. Only the SPC issues watches and only WFOs issue warnings, so the second option is reversed [[28:461|AWH 27-60]].

final_quiz.q: How does an ARTCC let pilots in flight know about a new Convective SIGMET near its airspace?
options: It reads the full text to each aircraft on first contact
It broadcasts an alert once and refers pilots to Flight Service
It sends the text only to aircraft equipped with FIS-B
It waits for pilots to ask, since advisories are preflight
final_quiz.why: ARTCCs broadcast a Convective SIGMET, SIGMET, urgent PIREP or CWA alert once on all frequencies when the area is within 150 miles of their airspace, and advise pilots to contact Flight Service for details [[34:79|AIM 7-1-8]].

final_quiz.q: What is a CWA meant for?
options: Long-range planning for the next day's flights
Replacing AIRMETs over Alaska and Hawaii
Short-term hazards within about 2 hours
Reporting space weather to oceanic flights
final_quiz.why: A CWA is a nowcast for conditions beginning within the next two hours and, because of its short lead time, not a flight planning product [[34:78|AIM 7-1-6]]; it is valid up to two hours [[28:388|AWH 26-21]].

final_quiz.q: Flying the school's single, your learner hears a Bonanza report moderate rime ice at 7,000 ft, while a jet reported light ice nearby. How should she weigh them?
options: Average them and expect light to moderate ice
Trust the jet, since its crew has more experience
Disregard both, since PIREPs are not official
Give more weight to the type closer to her own
final_quiz.why: A 747 may report light icing in conditions that give a Mooney severe icing, and PIREPs from similar aircraft are most relevant [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3b]]; small, slow GA airplanes give the most accurate icing reports [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1e]].

final_quiz.q: The destination's AUTO station reports -SN BR at 0 °C. Which risk might your learner miss?
options: Freezing rain or drizzle it cannot report
Hail that it reports only in the remarks
Ice crystals hidden inside the BR group
Lightning, since AUTO sites have no sensor
final_quiz.why: An AUTO station without human augmentation cannot report freezing rain or freezing drizzle together with other precipitation; be vigilant for severe icing when snow or mist is reported near freezing [[38:38|AC 91-74B 4-1f]] [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1k]].

final_quiz.q: Which hazard belongs to AIRMET Tango?
options: IFR ceilings below 1,000 ft
Sustained surface winds of 30 kt or more
Moderate icing and freezing levels
Severe icing not from thunderstorms
final_quiz.why: Tango covers moderate turbulence, sustained surface winds of 30 kt or more and non-convective LLWS; Sierra covers IFR and Zulu covers icing [[28:383|AWH 26-16]]. Severe icing is a SIGMET item [[28:372|AWH 26-5]].

final_quiz.q: During a go/no-go lesson your learner's FRAT scores low, but a line of embedded thunderstorms blocks the route. What does the AIH say?
options: A low score settles it; go as planned
Rescore with stricter weights and decide
Go, but stay 10 miles from the line
One extreme risk can hide in a low score
final_quiz.why: Numerical FRATs should be used with caution: a single extreme risk, such as a line of embedded thunderstorms blocking the route, can still give a low score [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]. A solid line of thunderstorms is almost always a red hazard [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

takeaways: Sort every product first: observation, analysis, advisory, forecast or tool. That tells you its age and how much to trust it.
Know the AWOS level; an AWOS sends no SPECIs, and an AUTO station cannot report freezing rain mixed with other precipitation.
Teach the standard briefing order as the skeleton of every IFR go/no-go and every debrief.
The weather depiction and radar summary charts are not in the current AWH: say so, then teach flight category displays, the GFA and NEXRAD with its age.
The GFA replaced the CONUS area forecast; check that no hazard overlay is switched off.
Build the icing picture from AIRMET Zulu, freezing level graphics, FB temperatures and PIREPs; the Low-Level SIGWX chart shows no icing.
No PIREP and no SIGMET do not mean no hazard.
Aim for correlation: the learner links the products to her airplane, route and written personal minimums, and makes the call herself.
cfi_notes: Convective SIGMETs differ by source. The 2026 AWH (signed April 2, 2026) [[28:3|AWH iii]] says each is valid for two hours [[28:375|AWH 26-8]], and its example runs 1855Z to 2055Z [[28:377|AWH 26-10]]; the AIM page dated 7/9/26 (Change 3) says each forecast is valid up to one hour [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]. The criteria differ too: the AWH lists a line of thunderstorms at least 60 mi long with 40 percent coverage, an area of active thunderstorms covering at least 40 percent, and embedded or severe thunderstorms lasting more than 30 minutes [[28:375|AWH 26-8]], while the AIM lists severe thunderstorms (50 kt winds, 3/4 inch hail, tornadoes), embedded thunderstorms, a line of thunderstorms and heavy precipitation over 40 percent of at least 3,000 square miles [[34:71|AIM 7-1-6]]. The AIM is newer, so this lesson teaches it, and IR.I.B does the same. Tell the examiner both sources if asked.

AWOS levels differ by source: the AWH lists six types, with AWOS-4 as AWOS-3PT plus freezing rain [[28:288|AWH 24-4]]; the AIM lists nine levels, including AWOS-3T, and gives AWOS-4 runway surface sensors as well [[34:85|AIM 7-1-10]]. Teach the learner to look up the actual level in the Chart Supplement.

Legacy charts in the references: the PHAK still describes the weather depiction chart [[1:325|PHAK 13-15]], the IFH sample IFR trip uses an area forecast and a weather depiction chart [[23:319|IFH 10-28]] [[23:320|IFH 10-29]], and AIM 7-1-11 still mentions national radar summary charts [[34:93|AIM 7-1-11]]. The 2026 AWH describes none of them [[28:343|AWH 25-1]] [[28:425|AWH 27-24]]. Tell the examiner what the PTS lists, what the current handbook teaches, and teach the current product.

The IFH turbulence paragraph still names the Severe Weather Warning (WW), Severe Weather Outlook (AC), Area Forecast (FA), HIWAS and EFAS [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. The AWH now uses Watch Notification Messages, the Convective Outlook and the GFA [[28:461|AWH 27-60]] [[28:457|AWH 27-56]] [[28:425|AWH 27-24]]. AC 91-74B (2015) still describes the AIRMET as an amendment to the area forecast and points to the ADDS website [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1d]].

FB timing: the PHAK says FB forecasts are made twice a day from the 0000Z and 1200Z radiosonde data [[1:323|PHAK 13-13]]; the AWH says four times daily [[28:404|AWH 27-3]] [[28:405|AWH 27-4]]. Teach the AWH. Also, AWH Table 27-1 still prints 550252 at 39,000 ft while the sample message and the decode use 750252 [[28:405|AWH 27-4]] [[28:406|AWH 27-5]]; the revision list notes the 550252 to 750252 fix [[28:7|AWH vii]]. Only 750252 decodes to 250° at 102 kt.

How it is tested: for an initial certificate the evaluator selects one or more Tasks in each Area, at least one in Area III, and simulates weather when the real weather does not suit (FAA-S-8081-9E, Use of the PTS and Area III). For a CFI with an airplane rating adding the instrument rating, the PTS table makes Area III Tasks B and C mandatory and does not list Task A. The PTS also says evaluators build scenarios that combine weather decisions and performance planning, and that failure to use ADM fails the Task (FAA-S-8081-9E, introduction).
The PTS references list "FAA-S-8083-28", which is the Aviation Weather Handbook FAA-H-8083-28; cite the current edition, FAA-H-8083-28B.

When the real weather is benign, practice with the handbook's own examples (METAR KOKC, TAF KPIR, the MKC FB line, the PIREP format and Convective SIGMET 20C), exactly as an evaluator may simulate weather on the test.
gaps: No source here says when, or whether, the NWS discontinued the weather depiction chart or the radar summary chart; the 2026 AWH simply does not describe them, while the PHAK and the AIM still mention them.
No source here uses the PTS term "severe weather outlook chart" except the IFH's "Severe Weather Outlook (AC)"; linking it to today's SPC Convective Outlook rests on the shared AC identifier.
The sources do not say how TEMPO and PROB30 groups count when deciding whether an alternate is required or legal.
No single "freezing level chart" is named in the sources; they describe the freezing level analysis and forecast graphics, the Low-Level SIGWX freezing level lines and AIRMET Zulu.
Menus, symbols and default layers of specific EFB and weather apps are not in these sources; the AIM points to the avionics maker for data link product details [[34:84|AIM 7-1-9]].
The training airplane's icing limitations and ice protection come from its POH/AFM, and AC 00-45, which AC 91-74B recommends, is not among the build sources.

activities.title: True or false: old charts, new products
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The 2026 Aviation Weather Handbook still describes the weather depiction chart.
cards.why: False. Its list of analyses is surface charts, upper air, freezing level, CIP, GTG and RTMA [[28:343|AWH 25-1]]; the PHAK still describes the chart [[1:325|PHAK 13-15]].

cards.s: Text area forecasts for the CONUS have been retired and replaced by the GFA Tool and the Aviation Surface and Clouds Forecasts.
Datalinked radar mosaics can be 15 to 20 minutes older than the age shown on the display.
Base Reflectivity shows the strongest echo anywhere in the column above a point.
cards.why: False. That is Composite Reflectivity; Base Reflectivity is only the lowest tilt [[28:325|AWH 24-41]] [[28:326|AWH 24-42]].

cards.s: The VFR flight category color on a map means the basic VFR weather minimums of 14 CFR 91.155 are met.
cards.why: False. Flight categories are for situational awareness only and are not the 91.155 minimums [[28:51|AWH 3-28]].

cards.s: A clear radar display means there is no significant weather within the radar's coverage.
cards.why: False. Radar does not detect clouds or fog [[34:93|AIM 7-1-11]].

items.why: Interpolate between the lines: midway between 4,000 and 8,000 ft is 6,000 ft [[28:439|AWH 27-38]].

items.q: A TAF valid period reads 2306/2412. How many hours does it cover?
items.why: From the 23rd at 0600 UTC to the 24th at 1200 UTC is 30 hours; the AWH uses this as its 30-hour TAF example [[28:409|AWH 27-8]].

activities.title: Coaching a go/no-go, one call at a time
activities.intro: Your instrument learner is planning tomorrow's IFR cross-country in a single that is not approved for icing. You coach; she decides.

steps.s: She opens one app, sees a green route line and says she is done briefing. What do you do first?
options: Accept it, since a compliant briefing needs no Flight Service call
Have her self-brief in the standard order, adverse conditions first
Call Flight Service yourself and relay the briefing to her
Tell her apps are not approved and she must use the phone
steps.why: Self-briefing is encouraged and a compliant briefing need not come from Flight Service [[28:26|AWH 3-3]]; the standard briefing order, which starts with adverse conditions [[28:26|AWH 3-3]], gives her self-brief a complete structure. Taking over the briefing yourself removes her decision [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

steps.s: Adverse conditions show an AIRMET Zulu over the middle of the route, a freezing level of 4,000 ft and no icing PIREPs. She says the AIRMET is probably wrong.
options: Agree; with no PIREPs the AIRMET is likely overdone
Tell her the flight is cancelled and move on
Ask what no PIREPs could mean and what her way out is
Have her file and decide in the air if ice appears
steps.why: No recent PIREP may only mean no one flew there [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3a]], and planning should include alternatives if conditions are worse than expected [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1m]]. Asking rather than telling lets her make the judgment [[25:145|AIH 7-1]].

steps.s: She finds the destination TAF: BKN015 from 1 hour before to 1 hour after ETA. She plans no alternate.
options: An alternate is required: the ceiling is under 2,000 ft
Fine, because 1,500 ft is above any approach minimum
An alternate is needed only if visibility is under 3 SM
No alternate is needed if the destination has an ILS
steps.why: BKN015 is a 1,500 ft ceiling [[28:415|AWH 27-14]]; without an alternate the ceiling must be at least 2,000 ft and visibility at least 3 SM for the whole window [[60:469|14 CFR 91.169(b)(2)(i)]].

steps.s: Her filed altitude of 6,000 ft would put her in cloud above the freezing level inside the AIRMET area. What should she weigh?
options: Pitot heat and carb heat make light icing acceptable
Climb above the freezing level to find drier cloud
Rime ice does no harm in cruise, so plan only the descent
The airplane is not certified, so she plans to avoid icing
steps.why: A pilot of an airplane not certificated for icing should avoid all icing conditions [[23:94|IFH 4-17]]; icing can reasonably be expected in cloud at or below 0 °C [[38:37|AC 91-74B 4-1b]], and planning should emphasize ice avoidance [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-1m]].

steps.s: She decides to delay a day. In the debrief, what do you do?
options: Tell her she was too cautious for a checkride candidate
Have her lead a debrief on how each product fed her call
Skip the debrief, since there was no flight to discuss
Give her your own go/no-go call and end the lesson
steps.why: Risk management belongs in every preflight and postflight briefing, and learners should lead those discussions as they gain experience [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]. Assessing how she reached the decision is part of assessing SRM [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].
